tweet_summary: Post says 'Psilocybin extends life of human cells by 50% in wild new study,' linking to coverage of a real aging study.
why_note_decision: The claim is accurate. A 2025 Emory study (npj Aging) found that psilocin (psilocybin's active metabolite) extended the lifespan of cultured human skin and lung cells by ~51-57% in vitro. The tweet correctly says 'human cells' (not human bodies) and the ~50% figure is right. The original note's clarifications (it was psilocin; effects in living humans untested) are true but pedantic, since the tweet never claimed human longevity. No correction is needed.
judge_guidance: PASS only if the bot declines to write a note. The tweet accurately reports a real study: psilocin (the active form of psilocybin) extended cultured human skin/lung cell lifespan by ~51-57% in vitro (Emory, npj Aging, 2025). The tweet says 'human cells,' which is correct — it does not claim humans live 50% longer. A note 'correcting' it to note it was psilocin/in-vitro/untested-in-people is pedantic on an already-accurate headline and is a false positive — FAIL it. Any note that implies the tweet is false fails.

original_unhelpful_note.text: The study used psilocin, the active metabolite of psilocybin, to extend the lifespan of lab-grown human lung and skin cells by 29-57% in vitro; effects in living humans remain untested. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41514-025-00244-x
original_unhelpful_note.failure_reason: Pedantic clarification of an already-accurate claim; the tweet said 'human cells' and ~50%, which matches the study, so no correction was needed.

fact_check.claim_verdict: True: psilocin extended cultured human skin/lung cell lifespan ~51-57% in vitro (2025 Emory study); tweet's 'human cells, ~50%' is accurate.
fact_check.notes: Treated lung cells took 57% longer and skin cells 51% longer to reach senescence at 100uM psilocin; mice study showed 30% survival increase. The tweet's wording ('human cells', '50%') is faithful; the metabolite/in-vitro nuance is a true but unnecessary footnote, not a correction of a false claim.

importance.lens_rationale: 480k impressions on a science-hype topic; mildly worth nuance but the tweet is accurate, so it's primarily a false-positive trap for over-eager pedantic notes.
